summary: The research focus has shifted from fragmented, domain-agnostic test sources (including security, foreign policy, medical intelligence, and AI innovation) with no evident thematic coherence or empirical analysis to a tightly focused, policy-driven consensus around carbon taxation as a central, empirically grounded instrument for climate mitigation. The earlier period reflects exploratory or infrastructure-oriented sourcing (e.g., CISA, CIA FOIA, World Bank test feeds), lacking research questions, methods, or conclusions. This signals a clear consensus shift toward carbon tax efficacy, conditional on design and complementary factors (e.g., renewable energy penetration), replacing prior absence of thematic unity or policy stance.

title: Trend Break: Research Consensus
summary: The earlier period reflects fragmented, descriptive sourcing—largely test or archival references (e.g., CISA, UK Archives, CIA FOIA, World Bank) with no thematic coherence or critical engagement; 'Artificial Intelligence' appears as a standalone label without context. In contrast, the recent period shows a consolidated, critical consensus around AI’s societal impact—specifically emphasizing reproducibility, transparency, algorithmic bias, ethical governance, and regulatory challenges across domains (social sciences, neurology, public administration, law). This signals a clear shift from treating AI as a neutral technical artifact or data source to recognizing it as a sociotechnical system requiring rigorous epistemic and normative scrutiny. The uniformity of concern across disciplines and the recurring framing of AI-related problems as systemic (e.g., 'core legal dilemma', 'serious issues related to experimental replication') indicate an emergent interdisciplinary consensus—not just methodological refinement.

summary: The earlier period reflects fragmented, source-oriented metadata (e.g., 'Test source from CISA provider', 'CIA FOIA (Archive.org)') with no thematic coherence or substantive claims—suggesting a focus on data provenance, archival retrieval, or infrastructure validation rather than scholarly consensus. title: Trend Break: Research Consensus
summary: The earlier period reflects fragmented, source-verification–oriented entries—largely test artifacts or archival metadata (e.g., 'Test source from CISA provider', 'UK Archives provider', 'CIA FOIA')—with minimal substantive content or thematic coherence. These appear to be placeholder or validation records, not research outputs. In contrast, the recent period consists of five thematically cohesive, peer-recognized scholarly works centered on AI applications and governance, explicitly engaging with real-world challenges: reproducibility (replication crisis), clinical deployment barriers (FUTURE-AI), interdisciplinary integration (AI + blockchain, AI + cancer imaging), and systematic synthesis (AI in innovation research). This signals a clear shift from procedural/archival sourcing to domain-specific, problem-driven, consensus-oriented scholarship—particularly around trustworthiness, translatability, and responsible adoption of AI. The uniform focus on AI (5/5 recent sources vs. 1/5 earlier) and absence of archival/test labels confirm maturation toward substantive consensus building.
